analysis.one_liner: Extends the 36% interest-rate cap and lending protections now limited to military families to all borrowers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2026 with 16 Senate Democrats and no Republicans behind it, the bill has sat in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Servicemembers are already protected by the Military Lending Act: lenders cannot charge them more than a 36% annual percentage rate once fees are counted, and certain loan practices are banned outright. This bill would apply those same rules to every consumer credit transaction, with carve-outs for home mortgages, car-purchase loans secured by the car, and federal credit unions. It also blocks the consumer bureau from granting industry exemptions and lets state attorneys general and regulators sue to enforce it. The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary borrowers who use short-term and high-cost credit — payday and auto-title loan customers, subprime installment borrowers, and people carrying high-rate credit card balances. Under the bill, the all-in cost of that credit, including most fees, could not exceed 36% a year, and the same loan-practice bans that protect troops would apply to them.

how_it_helps.text: Applies section 987(b) of title 10 — the Military Lending Act's rate and terms limits — to any creditor extending consumer credit to any consumer, not just covered servicemembers and dependents.

Requires that the annual percentage rate on open-end credit be calculated under the Defense Department's 2015 rules, which count most fees and add-on charges toward the capped rate, closing the gap between the advertised rate and the true cost.

Prohibits the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from using its exemption authority to waive these rules, and gives state attorneys general and state regulators standing to sue violators within three years.
Preserves stronger state consumer-protection laws and applies the Military Lending Act's civil penalties and remedies to violations against any consumer.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost lenders: payday, title, and subprime installment companies whose business model depends on triple-digit all-in rates, and card issuers whose APRs exceed the cap. Some borrowers with poor credit could also pay in the form of reduced access to credit at any price if lenders exit that market rather than lend at 36%.

drawbacks.text: A 36% all-in cap can make short-term lending to the riskiest borrowers uneconomic, so some lenders may simply stop making those loans; borrowers who rely on them could lose access to credit entirely or be pushed toward unregulated lenders — the same tradeoff Congress weighed when it applied these rules to the military.

The bill exempts residential mortgages and car-purchase loans secured by the vehicle, and leaves federal credit unions outside the cap, so some of the most expensive forms of consumer debt — including many fees tacked onto car loans — remain outside the new limit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and large: the Military Lending Act's fee-inclusive 36% cap has prevented lenders from burying troops in stacked fees and triple-digit effective rates, and this bill extends that same protection to everyone. The honest cost is that some marginal borrowers may find no lawful lender willing to serve them at 36%, which is why the military version was defended as necessary for a captive population. On balance, borrowers gain price protection that currently exists only for servicemembers, and the state-enforcement and no-exemption provisions make the cap harder to erode.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee on February 5, 2026, and there has been no hearing, committee vote, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the Predatory Lending Elimination Act on February 5, 2026; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill would extend the Military Lending Act's consumer-credit protections, including its limitations on rates and loan terms, to all consumers rather than only servicemembers and their dependents.
Sixteen Senate Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The only actions in the bill's history are its introduction and committee referral — no hearings, markups, votes, or floor scheduling appear in the record.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost consumer lenders, who continue to operate under current rules and keep charging rates and fees the bill would have capped. Borrowers are no worse off than before, but they gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors are Senate Democrats; not one of the Senate's 55 Republicans signed on.

industries.industry: Payday, auto-title, and subprime installment lenders
industries.note: The bill extends the Military Lending Act's fee-inclusive 36% rate cap and loan-term limits to all consumers, which makes triple-digit-APR small-dollar lending uneconomic — the same rules that already apply to loans to troops. Their revenue depends on charges the bill would prohibit.

Issuers charging APRs above 36% would have to lower them, and credit insurance and ancillary-product fees would count toward the capped rate. But the bill lets card fees that comply with the Truth in Lending Act's fee rules stay outside the rate calculation, preserving much fee revenue for mainstream issuers whose rates are already under the cap.

Credit unions are carved out of the cap entirely, leaving them as one of the few remaining lawful sources of small-dollar credit at lower rates — a competitive advantage if commercial payday lenders exit the market.

Residential mortgages and car-purchase loans secured by the vehicle are explicitly exempted, so these lenders keep charging fees and add-ons the bill would restrict elsewhere — though that carve-out is also why many expensive car-loan charges stay legal.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and the Banking Committee controlled by the 55-member Republican majority, the bill is likely to sit without a hearing or vote for the remainder of this Congress, like most bills referred to committee; it would need renewed introduction to move in the next one.
